concept: A wall of identical lamps is driven by a hidden branching circuit. The player may inject colored test pulses at three junctions, observe which downstream lamps fail, then replace exactly one concealed component.
differentiator: Diagnosis requires choosing discriminating test locations; it is not a switch-per-lamp wiring puzzle.

concept: Two rail carts respond correctly alone but interfere when commands overlap. By scheduling short calibration motions, the player identifies the single shared control line and inserts an isolator before transporting fragile cargo.
differentiator: The defect appears only under simultaneous activation, separating interaction faults from broken parts.

concept: A tiled floor contains one cracked support whose load propagates through visible beams. Limited weighted probes reveal deformation patterns; the player must reinforce the actual crack rather than the tile that bends most.
differentiator: Observations are spatial fields generated by one latent defect, not binary hidden hazards.

concept: A clockwork wall has several meshed branches and one jammed axle. Turning chosen input wheels reveals partial motion and backlash; removing the wrong axle disconnects a required branch permanently.
differentiator: Backlash makes local nonmovement ambiguous until multiple inputs are compared.

concept: A closed pipe loop slowly loses colored fluid at one seam. The player places two movable gauges, cycles valves, and triangulates the leak from pressure drops before spending one patch.
differentiator: The leak is inferred from conservation residuals under changed valve configurations.

concept: A branching kinetic sculpture carries test marbles through hinged petals, but one hinge catches only when approached from one direction. The player launches marbles from several leaves and replaces the directional fault.
differentiator: A direction-specific mechanical fault defeats one-way testing and simple earliest-failure heuristics.

concept: Platforms sag as if an invisible weight were attached to one of several linked beams. Moving a standard weight among sockets changes the sag pattern, allowing the hidden attachment point to be inferred and detached.
differentiator: The diagnostic object is known; only its interaction with the latent load reveals structure.

concept: A machine fails after a rapid chain of ten visible events. The player can replay it and freeze one event per run, discovering which early deviation causes later alarms before replacing a single module.
differentiator: The first alarm is downstream of the causal deviation, so temporal proximity is misleading.

concept: A powered network must keep two sinks alive while the player reroutes one broken edge using a short cable. Disconnecting a live articulation point causes irreversible shutdown, so a temporary bypass must precede removal.
differentiator: Repair order matters because service continuity is part of the goal.

concept: Three machines lose one tile of track after each cycle. A tiny stock of universal track can be moved only while a machine is stopped; the player schedules preventive relocation so all machines finish their quotas.
differentiator: Resources are reusable but unavailable during operation, creating maintenance scheduling rather than permanent construction.

concept: A spreading overload travels through a visible circuit toward healthy districts. The player may cut two links and bridge one alternate route, isolating the damaged region without starving the goal district.
differentiator: Success requires containment plus preserved service, not merely stopping propagation.

concept: Rotating machinery exposes safe service openings on different phases. Worn parts visibly approach failure, and the player must choose which service to perform during each short opening before a final production run.
differentiator: The core problem is deadline-aware preventive maintenance under mutually exclusive windows.

concept: Four incomplete devices need three functions each, but spare modules are scarce. The player dismantles a nonessential device and redistributes compatible parts so a required subset can operate together.
differentiator: Components have interface constraints and one donor may sacrifice itself; this is repair through reconfiguration.

concept: A repair drone leaves curing sealant behind and cannot cross wet repairs. It must seal every crack in a chamber while preserving its own route to the exit and allowing repaired pressure zones to reactivate.
differentiator: Repair geometry changes navigability continuously, unlike ordinary visit-all paths.

concept: Two machines calibrate one another: each can measure the other but cannot measure itself. The player alternates adjustments while neither machine may leave its safe range for more than one turn.
differentiator: Mutual calibration creates a coupled repair process with temporary tolerance constraints.

concept: A modular vehicle begins losing components during travel. The player reroutes power and drops optional functions after each visible failure, preserving steering and braking long enough to reach the dock.
differentiator: There is no full repair; the task is maintaining a minimum viable capability set under progressive damage.

concept: Movement arrows are transformed by an unknown fixed reflection and rotation. A safe calibration pad permits three moves with visible displacement before the player crosses a hazard field where every mistake consumes terrain.
differentiator: The mapping is learned from action-outcome pairs, not inferred from camera orientation.

concept: A two-link arm has one joint wired with reversed direction and unknown zero orientation. The player tests it in free space, then threads the arm through narrow sockets without touching walls.
differentiator: Separate joint mappings must be composed into an end-effector model.

concept: Each directional command persists for an unknown number of ticks unless canceled by its opposite. A practice lane reveals the persistence; later lanes require braking early around moving obstacles.
differentiator: Control has memory, so identical commands produce different motion depending on recent input.

concept: Horizontal and vertical commands are independently permuted inside colored floor regions. Boundary markers show regime changes, and the player must carry a rolling object through several regions without stopping it.
differentiator: Mappings factor by axis and region instead of changing as one global rotation.

concept: A boat executes steering commands after a fixed but initially unknown delay shown through queued wake marks. The player estimates the delay in open water, then navigates a narrow moving channel.
differentiator: The action is correct but temporally displaced, demanding queue-aware control rather than remapping.

concept: The same push moves one, two, or three cells depending on an unknown soil zone. Movable test stones reveal local gain, after which fragile seeds must be positioned exactly without overshoot.
differentiator: Control magnitude varies spatially while direction stays stable.

concept: A slider ignores small repeated pushes until accumulated force crosses an unknown threshold, then jumps by the excess. The player identifies thresholds for several sliders and aligns them without collision.
differentiator: Subthreshold actions alter latent actuator state despite no visible movement.

concept: Every move combines the command with a constant hidden drift whose direction changes only between levels. A sheltered strip exposes pure commands, while flags outside reveal net displacement through the field.
differentiator: The player must separate actuator mapping from an additive environmental disturbance.

concept: Two identical cursors move, but only one responds directly; the other follows a deterministic autonomous rule. Cheap neutral actions identify the controlled cursor before either approaches irreversible switches.
differentiator: The unknown is ownership of effects, not object identity or appearance.

concept: Four floor buttons respond to pairs of directional inputs rather than single actions. The player discovers the chord-to-button binding, then activates a spatial sequence while avoiding forbidden chords.
differentiator: Primitive actions acquire effects only in simultaneous combinations.

concept: Commands produce immediate decoy flashes and delayed physical changes in different locations. Repeated timing comparisons reveal which delayed effect belongs to which command.
differentiator: Salient immediate feedback is explicitly noncausal, testing temporal binding.

concept: One pedal controls whichever machine currently has the lowest visible pressure, so its target changes after every use. The player must predict reassignment while balancing several machines.
differentiator: A stable action has a dynamically selected recipient rather than a fixed endpoint.

concept: Movement commands affect the last object touched by a roaming highlight that disappears after selection. The player tracks the latent selection while objects cross and later issues remote moves.
differentiator: Control state becomes invisible while appearance and positions continue changing.

concept: Control rotates among three bodies, but the ownership marker appears only on every fourth turn. The player infers the intervening rotation law and coordinates bodies onto simultaneous sockets.
differentiator: Agency must be propagated between sparse ownership observations.

concept: A lever alternates between pushing its near branch and pulling its far branch according to a hidden two-state actuator mode. Consequences reveal mode, but each consequence also changes the branch geometry.
differentiator: Inferring actuator state is entangled with changing world state.

concept: The player and two visible automatic controllers issue commands to one platform each turn. An unknown but stable priority rule resolves conflicts; the player must infer arbitration and exploit lower-priority commands as blockers.
differentiator: Observed motion is the result of command resolution, not any single policy.

concept: Two vertical wells expose only their top pieces. The player transfers colored shapes between wells and output sockets, using the wells as stacks to realize a target order without ever seeing buried pieces directly.
differentiator: The puzzle isolates LIFO state and temporary storage rather than physical packing.

concept: Seeds enter three opaque irrigation channels and emerge in insertion order after different visible delays. The player schedules arrivals so compatible plants meet at shared beds.
differentiator: FIFO order combines with channel latency; items cannot be reordered inside a channel.

concept: A circular rack holds the last six inserted tiles and overwrites the oldest when full. The player controls insertion and one-step rotation to present a requested stream at the output gate.
differentiator: Success depends on bounded overwrite semantics, not merely cyclic movement.

concept: Crates have visible size and hidden arrival color revealed only at the exit. Pairwise comparators may swap by size, but equal-size crates must preserve their original relative order to satisfy receivers.
differentiator: The target distinguishes stable sorting from any size-sorted permutation.

concept: Fruit values are encoded by area. The player may swap only parent-child positions in a tree and repeatedly harvest the root, maintaining a max-heap so every harvest is the current largest.
differentiator: Local structural invariants must be maintained across repeated removals.

concept: A narrow ferry accepts and releases cargo only at its two ends. Dock requests arrive spatially, and the player chooses front or back operations to serve them without moving internal cargo.
differentiator: Both ends are controllable but the interior remains inaccessible.

concept: Four visible registers hold shapes; the only operations swap adjacent registers or rotate three. The player must transform several start states with one reusable short operation sequence.
differentiator: A single program must generalize across inputs, excluding state-specific search traces.

concept: A head walks along a strip, reads colors, writes one of two marks, and changes its tiny visible internal state. The player configures a transition table geometrically so the autonomous head converts every input strip correctly.
differentiator: The artifact being built is a finite-state algorithm, not a path or physical tool.

concept: Two autonomous carriers read and write shared floor switches on the same ticks. The player inserts waits so their operations occur in a safe order and a gate sees both required states.
differentiator: Each carrier is correct alone; failure emerges only from an interleaving.

concept: Two workers need a one-cell tunnel and can deadlock face to face. Movable semaphore tokens are obeyed by both workers, and the player places them to guarantee exclusive passage under either arrival order.
differentiator: The solution must work for two visibly possible schedules, not one replayed timing.

concept: A bridge collapses if only one of two coupled locks changes before a cart crosses. The player may bundle selected switch changes into one atomic action using a limited clamp.
differentiator: Correct final switch states are insufficient; the transition itself must be indivisible.

concept: Three boats each hold one colored lock and request another. The player can order releases and grants but cannot force a boat to relinquish after it receives its second lock.
differentiator: Avoiding circular wait is the central mechanic; no route or collision solution bypasses it.

concept: Several agents traverse unequal loops and may wait at striped barriers. Opening a barrier releases every waiting agent together; the player uses barrier phases to align their final arrivals.
differentiator: Synchronization acts on a set of waiting processes rather than individual timers.

concept: Two weaving automata share a shuttle. The player may preempt either only at visible safe states, preserving its local pattern while the other uses the shuttle.
differentiator: Preemption carries resumable internal state and unsafe interruption consequences.

concept: Tiles first reserve destinations, then all prepared moves commit together. The player controls prepare and commit pulses so multiple bodies exchange places without conflicting reservations.
differentiator: Movement is explicitly split into intention and atomic realization.

concept: Two polite robots repeatedly step aside in mirrored directions and never pass. The player can alter one robot's short response rule once, breaking livelock without causing collision.
differentiator: Both agents keep moving and remain safe, so progress failure is not a deadlock.

concept: Items flow into branching bins whose finite capacities are visible. Closing downstream gates propagates congestion upstream, and the player meters releases to prevent the source from overflowing.
differentiator: Queue occupancy changes what upstream actions are possible; paths alone do not explain flow.

concept: Carts queue at a small street grid. Letting one cart enter a full downstream segment blocks the intersection and can freeze every route; the player controls lights to preserve empty escape cells.
differentiator: Local green-light progress can produce global gridlock through spillback.

concept: Three chutes feed one server. Urgent items visibly decay faster, but too many priority admissions starve ordinary items required for the final pattern.
differentiator: The scheduler must balance deadlines and starvation rather than sort one static list.

concept: A furnace consumes a fixed pulse whether processing one compatible tile or four. Arrivals have different cooling windows, so the player groups batches without letting rare tiles expire.
differentiator: Efficiency comes from batching under deadlines, not route minimization.

concept: Two service stations alternate fast and slow phases while arrivals continue. The player reroutes queues before rate changes, using visible phase cues to avoid oscillating overload.
differentiator: Capacity is time-varying and queues retain history across phases.

concept: Two endless lanes merge into one finite buffer. Receivers require a bounded alternation of colors, so the player meters entries to satisfy fairness while keeping the buffer nonempty.
differentiator: The goal constrains both throughput and service fairness over time.

concept: Tiles change color as they wait and become unusable after a visible age. The player may serve, reorder only at designated sidings, or discard a tile to protect later commitments.
differentiator: Queue position and item age are separate state variables with different costs.

concept: Downstream sockets emit requests only when empty; upstream machines can overproduce and jam shared buffers. The player learns to trigger production from demand signals and maintain a small circulating inventory.
differentiator: Production must be pulled by consumption rather than pushed whenever capacity exists.

concept: Heaters affect nearby tile temperatures with lag. A gate opens only when every sensor remains inside a colored band for several turns, requiring anticipation rather than one-frame matching.
differentiator: The target is sustained regulation of a delayed field, not reaching a threshold once.

concept: Three reservoirs exchange fluid while an intermittent pump adds volume. The player adjusts valves to keep all levels inside safe bands until the pump finishes.
differentiator: Actions redistribute a shared disturbance across coupled controlled variables.

concept: A beetle's speed is shown by its trail length while terrain slope adds acceleration. The player maintains a target speed through changing slopes using discrete throttle and brake pulses.
differentiator: The regulated quantity is velocity, not position, and terrain supplies a persistent disturbance.

concept: A load atop a pivot falls unless small cart motions keep its visible lean centered. The cart must also progress slowly to a destination without saturating either edge.
differentiator: Goal progress and stabilization compete on the same control channel.

concept: Two species reproduce and consume one another under visible local rules. The player opens migration valves to keep both populations within bands long enough to restore a habitat.
differentiator: Neither maximization nor elimination wins; feedback must regulate a coupled oscillatory system.

concept: Doors respond to temperature with different open and close thresholds. The player cycles one heater to maintain a traversable sequence, exploiting the memory band instead of chasing exact values.
differentiator: Identical current temperatures can imply different door states because history matters.

concept: A greenhouse display shows moisture from three turns ago while irrigation acts immediately. The player learns the display lag and avoids overwatering a moving plant bed.
differentiator: Both actuator and sensor are reliable, but their timestamps differ.

concept: Two automatic regulators each stabilize one side of a shared platform but fight when tuned aggressively. The player selects among visible gain tiles so the combined system settles.
differentiator: Individually sensible controllers create oscillation through coupling.

concept: A rotating spoke appears to turn forward, stop, or reverse under different strobe intervals. The player changes the sampling pulse, infers true rotation, then couples the wheel at the correct phase.
differentiator: Observation frequency changes apparent dynamics while the underlying motion remains fixed.

concept: Several insects move on different short periods but are visible only on chosen flash turns. A limited flash schedule must reveal enough phase information to place one intercept net.
differentiator: Sampling times, not viewing locations, determine identifiability.

concept: A bridge alternates among load shapes faster than the default observation rhythm. The player may double or halve the viewing interval and must identify the true cycle before sending a cart.
differentiator: A safe decision requires selecting a sufficient sampling rate, not predicting from default frames.

concept: Two hidden rotors expose markers only when their phases coincide, producing a slow beat. The player infers their small frequency difference and schedules a transfer at the next coincidence.
differentiator: Long apparent periodicity arises from two nearby fast cycles.

concept: A target moves with constant velocity and occasional visible boundary bounces. The player can reveal it on only four turns, then must place a catcher at a future position.
differentiator: Sparse samples support trajectory estimation; exhaustive visibility is impossible.

concept: A camera can take short noisy-looking snapshots or long exposures that smear moving objects into paths. The player chooses exposure length to distinguish speed classes and open matching gates.
differentiator: Observation duration trades instantaneous position for integrated motion evidence.

concept: A field changes rarely but rapidly. Periodic probes waste a tiny battery, while a peripheral indicator can trigger a full observation after likely change events.
differentiator: The player designs event-triggered sampling rather than fixed-rate polling.

concept: Two fine stripe fields overlap to create a coarse moving pattern. The player shifts one field and uses the emergent bands to steer particles through otherwise invisible microchannels.
differentiator: The useful signal is an interference artifact of spatial sampling, not either layer alone.

concept: Four rigid links form a closed mechanism. Moving one accessible joint traces a constrained path that must carry a latch around an obstacle and into a socket.
differentiator: Closed-chain constraints determine motion; parts cannot be positioned independently.

concept: A legged machine advances only when two crank phases produce a stable foot trajectory. The player adjusts link holes and phase offset, then lets it cross uneven ground.
differentiator: Locomotion emerges from mechanism geometry instead of direct body movement.

concept: Interchangeable cam silhouettes convert one rotating input into different follower motions. The player selects and phases cams so flowers are pressed in a required temporal pattern.
differentiator: Tool shape specifies an entire motion profile, not a single affordance.

concept: A stacked scissor mechanism raises cargo while widening its base and amplifying small horizontal motion. The player chooses actuation points to clear ledges without exceeding side boundaries.
differentiator: Vertical reach, lateral footprint, and actuation displacement are geometrically coupled.

concept: A bent shaft transmits rotation through two jointed axes, but output phase varies with bend angle. The player aligns intermediate yokes so a distant pointer tracks evenly.
differentiator: Orientation and phase transmission matter jointly across a spatial linkage.

concept: A pantograph copies cursor motion at an unknown scale and reflection determined by pivot placement. The player calibrates it, then traces a target contour with the remote tip while the cursor avoids obstacles.
differentiator: One linked mechanism simultaneously transforms scale, orientation, and reachable space.

concept: A rotating crank drives a slider whose speed varies across the cycle. Timed slider contact must launch objects at two different speeds using only crank phase choices.
differentiator: Equal angular steps create unequal linear displacement.

concept: Three tendons curl multiple finger joints with overlapping effects. The player learns the coupling and grasps irregular objects without crushing marked fragile regions.
differentiator: Fewer actuators than joints create coordinated but nonindependent motion.

concept: An arch remains unstable until one wedge closes its force path. The player temporarily supports pieces, removes the supports in order, and tests whether the freestanding structure carries a rolling load.
differentiator: Correct geometry is not enough; construction and support-removal sequence determine stability.

concept: A roof load propagates through colored compression traces. Limited braces can redirect the trace around weak cells to the foundation without any member exceeding its capacity.
differentiator: The object of planning is an invisible-to-visible force path, not physical connectivity alone.

concept: A platform extends over a void and tilts according to cargo distance from its support. The player shuttles several loads across while movable counterweights occupy scarce deck space.
differentiator: Moment arm matters more than total mass, distinguishing torque from simple weight balance.

concept: A dense triangular frame contains decorative and essential bars. The player must remove enough bars to pass a vehicle through while preserving a rigid path under several load directions.
differentiator: The task asks which structure can be removed safely, not which pieces to add.

concept: Thin columns support equal loads but buckle along their weak orientation. The player rotates and laterally braces them so a descending press reaches full force.
differentiator: Strength depends on orientation and unsupported length rather than color-coded capacity.

concept: A tower sways left and right under a visible alternating load. One-way tension braces work only in pull, so paired diagonals must be arranged to resist both phases.
differentiator: Members have directional structural function under changing loads.

concept: Bridge piers on soft islands sink by visible amounts after each placed span. The player sequences spans and shims so the final deck becomes level only after settlement.
differentiator: Construction actions alter future support heights through accumulated load.

concept: A tall stack can be carried only by sliding foundation tiles underneath it one at a time. The projected center must remain inside the current support polygon during every intermediate move.
differentiator: Stability is constrained throughout a base-reconfiguration sequence, not just at endpoints.

concept: A patterned cloth stretches around pegs and retains a fraction of deformation after release. Repeated pulls train a permanent crease pattern that must fit a rigid frame.
differentiator: Material history accumulates continuously across otherwise reversible-looking manipulations.

concept: A soft object can squeeze through narrow locks but expands into side cavities. The player controls compression direction and timing so its final expanded outline contacts all required pins.
differentiator: Passage and activation depend on different deformed states of one object.

concept: Fluid travels through a flexible tube whose cross-section narrows under movable clamps and bulges elsewhere. The player shapes pressure and timing to split one pulse among receivers.
differentiator: Geometry responds to flow and then changes the flow, forming a material-fluid coupling.

concept: A sheet may be folded along any grid line, but repeated folds weaken a crease into a permanent hinge. The player creates just enough hinges for a later autonomous folding sequence.
differentiator: Repeated use changes the operation set by modifying material memory.

concept: A blob behaves rigidly under rapid pushes but slowly flows under sustained pressure. The player alternates impulses and waiting to cross gaps while retaining cargo on top.
differentiator: The same force produces different deformation depending on duration.

concept: Moving one node deforms an entire net. The player catches falling objects in marked pockets while keeping every strand below a visible tension limit.
differentiator: Local manipulation has global smooth effects and distributed constraints.

concept: A soft roadway springs back under light rollers but permanently dents under heavy ones. The player uses chosen loads to sculpt ramps without making impassable pits.
differentiator: Elastic and permanent deformation coexist around a learnable yield threshold.

concept: Compressed pieces are held by removable pins and expand along constrained paths when released. The player orders releases so recovering shapes push one another into sockets rather than jam.
differentiator: Stored deformation becomes an actuator whose effect depends on release order and confinement.

concept: A pulse reflects between movable walls. The player adjusts wall spacing so stable bright antinodes land on several receivers while dark nodes protect fragile tiles.
differentiator: Success depends on a spatial standing-wave pattern, not routing a ray to endpoints.

concept: Pulses reflect with or without color inversion depending on hidden wall material revealed only through returned echoes. The player diagnoses boundaries and schedules a final pulse that cancels at one branch and reinforces at another.
differentiator: Boundary conditions alter phase, so equal path length does not imply equal arrival effect.

concept: Two sources emit identical waves. The player offsets their start phases to suppress vibration at a bridge while preserving a strong signal at a distant gate.
differentiator: One source configuration must create cancellation and reinforcement at different locations.

concept: A wide channel supports two visible transverse patterns, and narrow junctions pass only one. Rotating short guide sections converts modes so energy reaches selected branches.
differentiator: Connectivity is unchanged; propagation depends on wave mode compatibility.

concept: Waves spread after apertures by amounts determined by gap width. The player sizes two openings to illuminate hidden-side receivers while leaving a central absorber dark.
differentiator: Narrower passages can spread influence more widely, opposing ray-like intuition.

concept: A pulse crossing abrupt material changes partly reflects. The player inserts intermediate layers whose visible stiffness gradually matches both sides, transmitting enough energy to open a gate.
differentiator: Adding material improves transmission by matching interfaces rather than shortening a path.

concept: A chamber amplifies only one of several input rhythms determined by its geometry. The player tests short rhythms, modifies one wall, and excites the new resonant mode without triggering neighboring chambers.
differentiator: Geometry selects temporal frequency and can be deliberately retuned.

concept: Different color components travel at different speeds through a channel. The player chooses their initial spacing so they recombine into one packet exactly at a moving receiver.
differentiator: The solution precompensates for predictable dispersion rather than merely synchronizing emission times.

concept: Irregular translucent patches must cover every marked cell exactly once; overlaps turn cells invalid and holes remain visible. Later levels allow patch rotation but introduce mandatory anchor contacts.
differentiator: The goal distinguishes exact cover from maximal area filling.

concept: Objects occupy a small depth stack, and two side projections specify allowed silhouettes. The player packs all objects so neither projection contains gaps or excess cells.
differentiator: Packing is constrained by multiple projections without reconstructing a single predetermined tower.

concept: Hollow cargo pieces can contain smaller pieces, changing their effective footprint and weight. The player nests and places everything into a hold with both space and balance constraints.
differentiator: Containment alters the packing items themselves rather than merely their positions.

concept: A rectangular floor can be divided only by full straight cuts. Given a set of target rectangles, the player chooses a recursive cut tree that produces all pieces without leftovers.
differentiator: Not every geometric tiling is reachable under guillotine-cut constraints.

concept: Rigid panels connected by hinges must fold into a compact shape inside a bin. The player may rotate joints only while swept areas remain clear.
differentiator: Feasible final shapes can still be unreachable because folding paths collide.

concept: A few sentry pieces sweep repeating visible footprints. The player chooses their start phases and locations so every target cell is visited within a window while no forbidden cell is ever visited.
differentiator: Coverage is accumulated over time by moving footprints rather than static placement.

concept: Screens must hide every fragile object from rotating emitters while leaving every solar receiver visible for at least one phase. A screen may help one phase and hurt another.
differentiator: The covered sets are phase-dependent visibility regions, not occupied cells.

concept: Cargo is packed into several depth layers, but a later retrieval sequence is shown spatially. The player must fit everything while ensuring each requested piece is exposed when needed.
differentiator: Packing quality includes future accessibility, preventing dense but unusable solutions.

concept: Agents display preferences through geometric proximity demonstrations. The player constructs pairs, and any mutually preferred unmatched pair visibly defects, so the final assignment must be stable.
differentiator: The criterion is absence of blocking pairs, not maximizing individual matches.

concept: Colored workers each fit several machines, while machines have capacities and require mixed skill shapes. The player assigns everyone so all lower quotas and compatibility constraints hold.
differentiator: Recipients accept sets with composition constraints, not single interchangeable occupants.

concept: Compatibility edges rotate after each work phase. The player may move only two assignments between phases, so the initial matching must anticipate future edge changes.
differentiator: Assignment quality is measured across a sequence with limited recourse.

concept: Stations request pairs of shapes whose joint pattern matters more than either shape. The player routes bundles through a swap market where breaking a useful pair can strand both components.
differentiator: Preferences are over combinations, defeating independent item matching.

concept: Two receivers value spatial features differently, as shown by prior choices. The player partitions indivisible tiles so neither receiver prefers the other's bundle and both minimum needs are met.
differentiator: The goal is relational fairness under inferred valuations, not equal counts.

concept: Carriers have different travel times to tasks. The player assigns all tasks so the slowest completion is as early as possible, with ties exposed by a final synchronized launch.
differentiator: The objective minimizes the worst assignment rather than total distance.

concept: Tasks occupy visible time intervals and require one of several rooms with different equipment. The player assigns rooms so overlapping tasks never conflict and every equipment need is met.
differentiator: Compatibility is temporal and resource-specific, not spatial adjacency.

concept: Every agent holds one object and wants another, but direct swaps are allowed only when both improve. The player identifies and triggers exchange cycles that clear all desires simultaneously.
differentiator: Progress may require a cycle commit because no pairwise trade is sufficient.

concept: Objects vary on several grounded visual relations. A gate accepts the unique object related correctly to every reference object except exactly one, with examples establishing the quantifier pattern.
differentiator: The category depends on counting relation violations, not matching surface features.

concept: Three-body relations such as spatial betweenness are demonstrated across rotated scenes. The player places a new body to satisfy several simultaneous ternary constraints.
differentiator: No pairwise relation alone determines the answer.

concept: A grid of agents must preserve row-based teams while ensuring no column repeats a learned functional role. Roles are inferred from behavior and survive appearance changes.
differentiator: Two equivalence relations must be satisfied simultaneously on different axes.

concept: Levers add or remove adjacency links. The target is a scene where each green object has exactly one red neighbor, while at least one blue object has none.
differentiator: Nested existence and uniqueness constraints are grounded in geometry.

concept: In a graph drawn as rooms and doors, the player marks every node whose neighbors all have at least one marked neighbor of another kind. Marks change the relation being evaluated.
differentiator: The property quantifies over neighbors of neighbors and is self-referential during construction.

concept: Observed moves demonstrate a directed reachability relation. The player adds the fewest shortcut links so every member of one region can reach every member of another.
differentiator: The relevant relation is path reachability, not direct adjacency.

concept: Each translucent triangle connects three cells that may not all share the same state. The player fills the board while satisfying overlapping triple constraints and fixed seeds.
differentiator: Constraints live on triples rather than ordinary neighboring pairs.

concept: A movable divider changes which objects count as neighbors. Each object's next state follows the majority relation in its region, and the player positions the divider to produce a target update.
differentiator: The action changes the quantified population before a simultaneous relational update.

concept: Several rooms are equivalent under rotation and reflection. The player must transform each into the same canonical orientation selected by an asymmetrically placed external anchor.
differentiator: Any equivalence is insufficient; the external anchor defines one reproducible representative.

concept: Identical agents on a symmetric ring exchange only neighbor pulses. One off-ring landmark breaks symmetry, and the player configures local rules so exactly one agent becomes leader.
differentiator: The task exposes why symmetry-breaking information is necessary for unique roles.

concept: A machine jams while several parts remain rotationally symmetric. The player may add one tiny marker whose position causes a deterministic scanner to visit every part exactly once.
differentiator: One low-bandwidth asymmetry changes global traversal behavior.

concept: Board transformations group cells into orbits. The player selects exactly one cell from each orbit, with later levels combining two generators rather than showing full symmetry.
differentiator: Coverage is over transformation equivalence classes rather than geometric regions.

concept: Identical robots begin in a symmetric chamber and follow the same commands. The player first changes the environment to create distinguishable local views, then assigns complementary jobs.
differentiator: Roles cannot be assigned until observations break anonymity.

concept: Several equal routes reach a gate, but downstream behavior requires every agent to choose the same one. The player arranges a geometric priority cue that consistently resolves otherwise exact ties.
differentiator: The environment tests construction of a shared canonical choice, not shortest-path discovery.

concept: A perfectly symmetric cellular pattern grows into repeated collisions. Adding one seed cell at the correct equivalence class breaks symmetry and yields a single traveling structure.
differentiator: A tiny initial asymmetry selects one macroscopic evolution among equivalent possibilities.

concept: Many sequences of reversible local rewrites produce equivalent diagrams. The player discovers a terminating orientation convention and reduces every diagram to the same normal form.
differentiator: The challenge is canonicalization under rewrites, not reaching one pictured target from one start.

concept: Each machine action has a visually demonstrated inverse, but the controls are unlabeled. The player returns several scrambled objects to origins by composing inferred inverses in reverse order.
differentiator: Reversal requires algebraic action order, not a dedicated undo button or time rewind.

concept: Two transformations individually preserve a lock pattern, yet applying A-B-A-inverse-B-inverse moves one hidden marker. The player exploits this commutator to isolate the marker without disturbing others.
differentiator: The useful effect exists only because operations do not commute.

concept: Several machines permute colors and positions. The player pairs each with its inverse by testing compositions, then routes cargo through pairs that restore appearance while changing location.
differentiator: Inverse identity is discovered through composition, not visual opposition.

concept: A familiar movement operation acts differently inside a rotated lattice. Wrapping it between entry and exit transformations reproduces the needed local move in global coordinates.
differentiator: The same operation is transported between representations through conjugation.

concept: The player connects swap and controlled-swap gates into a network that rearranges tokens yet can be run backward from any output. One-way merges are tempting but invalidate the test.
differentiator: Every intermediate transformation must preserve enough information for universal reversal.

concept: Available moves rotate overlapping subsets of pieces. The player identifies a small set of cycle generators and combines them to realize several requested permutations efficiently.
differentiator: Planning occurs in a generated transformation space rather than direct piece movement.

concept: A reversible sliding mechanism admits many arrangements but divides them into two unreachable classes. Demonstrations expose the invariant, and the player must choose which of two targets is actually reachable before acting.
differentiator: The main decision is algebraic reachability, preventing futile search toward an impossible target.

concept: A token's displayed pose represents the cumulative product of directional transformations. The player reaches a goal pose using a short word while canceling adjacent inverse pairs and exploiting repeated subwords.
differentiator: Spatial movement is a visualization of abstract transformation composition.

concept: Objects move after every action, but some displacement comes from the player's command and some from a periodic wind. Null actions and direction reversals let the player separate self-caused from external motion.
differentiator: The same observed transition contains both endogenous and exogenous causes.

concept: Several creatures move in apparent coordination. The player blocks selected creatures and discovers that one hidden controller drives a subset while the others merely follow local cues.
differentiator: Correlated agents may share a cause rather than communicate with one another.

concept: Two lamps always change together, suggesting a link. By shielding one upstream sensor, the player reveals their shared external trigger and routes a final signal correctly.
differentiator: Observation supports a false direct edge until a targeted intervention separates common cause from mediation.

concept: A floor pattern moves around the player as if chasing, but replaying the same route from a different start reveals a fixed reactive field. The player predicts it without assigning persistent goals.
differentiator: Goal-like behavior emerges from a stateless response rule.

concept: Among many moving pieces, exactly one is weakly steerable while all share similar trajectories. The player uses a few orthogonal commands to identify it and guide only that piece to a socket.
differentiator: Agency is identified by counterfactual controllability, not visual salience.

concept: An autonomous walker takes the same path toward one of several possible goals. The player moves one obstacle and observes replanning, distinguishing its goal from a memorized route before assisting it.
differentiator: Environmental intervention separates goal-directed planning from trajectory replay.

concept: The player can tag commands with colors, but each is executed by one of several devices after different delays. Matching delayed colored effects reveals which device each control influences.
differentiator: Explicit tags aid temporal attribution while heterogeneous delays prevent adjacency heuristics.

concept: A cluster contains limbs, carried tools, passengers, and nearby followers that all move partly together. The player probes joints and obstacles to infer which cells belong to the controllable body before fitting through a gate.
differentiator: Embodiment is discovered through intervention-dependent co-motion, not contiguous pixels.

concept: Training objects share overlapping subsets of features, but no single feature is necessary. The player routes new objects using graded family resemblance while rejecting a tempting one-feature rule.
differentiator: The class is prototype-like rather than a clean conjunction.

concept: Objects vary continuously in two spatial features. A few labeled examples define an oblique category boundary, and the player chooses informative queries before classifying a final batch.
differentiator: The relevant boundary combines features rather than thresholding either independently.

concept: A broad visual rule has a nested exception and an exception-to-the-exception, each introduced by demonstrations. The player classifies a final scene by applying the most specific matching rule.
differentiator: Category membership follows a specificity hierarchy, not a global regime change.

concept: The accepted object's appearance shifts slightly after every success. The player tracks a slowly moving category prototype while old examples remain displayed as stale evidence.
differentiator: The concept evolves locally rather than switching between discrete known rules.

concept: Positive examples form two visually distant clusters joined by a relational property; negative examples occupy the apparent middle. The player discovers the disjunctive rule and selects all members.
differentiator: A single similarity centroid misclassifies the category.

concept: An object's class depends on whether it is the smallest in its local group, not its absolute size. The player rearranges groups, causing category membership to change without changing any object.
differentiator: Membership is relational and context-sensitive rather than intrinsic.

concept: Solid pieces are categorized by the shape of the empty region they enclose. The player pairs visually dissimilar pieces that generate equivalent holes under rotation.
differentiator: The diagnostic feature is structured absence rather than filled pixels.

concept: Categories are taught through motion trajectories and tested on static spatial arrangements encoding the same relation graph. The player must preserve the concept across modalities.
differentiator: The transfer changes representation while retaining relational category structure.

concept: A maze gradually hides explored passages, but the player may leave a few movable frontier markers. Correct marker placement supports complete exploration without repeatedly traversing closed subtrees.
differentiator: The scarce resource represents search frontier state rather than map revelation.

concept: A scanner must observe every boundary segment of several irregular islands and return to its dock. Crossing an already scanned segment drains a shared battery, rewarding an organized survey rather than wandering.
differentiator: Coverage applies to object boundaries with costly retracing, not to visiting every floor cell.

concept: Partial construction branches display a guaranteed minimum remaining footprint. The player abandons branches whose bound already exceeds the best complete design and finds the smallest valid structure.
differentiator: Visible lower bounds make principled pruning the intended mechanic.

concept: A transformation maze is too deep from either end alone, but states reached from the start and target can be grown as colored frontiers until they meet.
differentiator: The target may be expanded backward using reversible transitions, rewarding meet-in-the-middle search.

concept: A large repetitive map has a few unique landmarks whose distance bands are visible. The player chooses which landmark relation to follow at each junction and reaches a hidden goal efficiently.
differentiator: Search guidance comes from relational landmark coordinates, not a complete map or gradient.

concept: A probe explores every action sequence up to a chosen depth and highlights whether a goal was found, but larger bounds cost sharply more. The player increases bounds carefully and then executes the discovered short plan.
differentiator: The environment makes depth limits explicit and rewards completeness without one huge search.

concept: A branching room repeats under rotations. The player identifies equivalent unexplored branches and marks one representative per symmetry class before a search automaton begins.
differentiator: Efficient coverage depends on quotienting symmetric branches, not canonicalizing final states.

concept: Each inspected region opens one new corridor and closes another according to a visible local rule. The player maintains a frontier of still-reachable unknown regions and avoids orphaning them.
differentiator: Exploration actions change future reachability without permanently consuming visited cells.

concept: Several visually different machine states produce identical responses to every available action. The player merges equivalent states into shared bins, then predicts transitions of the compressed machine.
differentiator: Equivalence is defined by future behavior, not visual or historical similarity.

concept: Rooms differ in decoration but share repeated transition structure. The player discovers equivalence classes and plans on the smaller quotient graph to reach any room with a target property.
differentiator: The route goal is class-based and efficient planning requires collapsing redundant concrete rooms.

concept: Every action randomly cycles decorative border colors while core object relations evolve deterministically. The player selects which state features to copy into a limited memory panel for later prediction.
differentiator: A high-change visual variable is causally irrelevant and competes for memory.

concept: A long observation stream drives a gate, but only one compact statistic of prior events determines the next state. The player builds a tiny memory machine that preserves exactly that statistic.
differentiator: Success requires discovering sufficient state rather than replaying or compressing the full history.

concept: The player groups observed configurations into a limited number of bins. Future transition tests reward groupings whose members have the same next-state distribution under every action.
differentiator: The abstraction is evaluated by predictive consistency across actions.

concept: Two differently rendered worlds expose related action graphs. The player pairs states so every move in one has a matching move in the other, then transfers a route.
differentiator: Correspondence requires reciprocal transition matching, stronger than one-way analogy.

concept: Fast internal particles cycle through many microstates while a slow machine mode changes only at specific aggregate patterns. The player samples and acts at the macro-state level.
differentiator: Many microstates share the same controllable future until a macro transition occurs.

concept: Two observations look identical but require different actions because of hidden history. The player chooses one additional sensor feature that splits only the aliased states while leaving other abstractions merged.
differentiator: The task refines an abstraction minimally instead of abandoning it wholesale.

concept: A gate states its requirement through several visual demonstrations of a relational property. Rather than answer yes or no, the player must construct one new configuration that visibly witnesses the property.
differentiator: Evaluation demands a constructive witness, excluding pattern recognition without synthesis.

concept: A proposed growth rule matches every displayed plant. The player receives a small edit budget and must create the smallest plant whose next growth contradicts the rule.
differentiator: The goal is targeted falsification, not discovering the true replacement rule.

concept: A large transformation is claimed impossible. The player selects a small colored substructure whose preserved parity or connectivity certifies that no action sequence can reach the target.
differentiator: An impossibility judgment must be accompanied by a visible invariant certificate.

concept: An overconstrained layout has no solution. The player highlights the smallest subset of translucent constraints that is already contradictory, causing the rest to fade.
differentiator: The output is a minimal explanation of failure rather than a near-solution.

concept: A maze route may pass through hidden one-way doors. The player lays a sparse sequence of checkpoint arrows such that a simple verifier can confirm every segment without replaying all movement.
differentiator: The artifact is a compact independently checkable certificate of reachability.

concept: A transport network fails a target property. The player removes irrelevant nodes until every remaining node is necessary for the failure, exposing a minimal obstruction.
differentiator: Understanding is measured by isolating the causal core, not repairing the network.

concept: Several candidate machines agree on common inputs but differ on edge cases. The player selects a tiny set of test patterns that distinguishes every pair before one unknown machine is presented.
differentiator: A test suite must cover a hypothesis set universally, not diagnose one known defect.

concept: A complex region is accepted only when partitioned into copies of a demonstrated primitive whose local validity is easy to see. The player supplies the decomposition as the proof.
differentiator: The solution carries its own spatial verification structure.

concept: A repeating spatial message loses one visibly blank packet per cycle. From cross-cycle redundancy, the player reconstructs each missing packet and triggers a receiver.
differentiator: Missing positions are known, so the challenge is erasure recovery rather than hidden-state search.

concept: Three relays carry transformed copies of the same geometric command, but one relay fails each level. The player combines any two consistent copies to recover the command.
differentiator: Redundancy spans independently transformed paths and must tolerate an absent channel.

concept: A channel corrupts one contiguous run of positions. The player interleaves neighboring parts of a picture before sending so the burst becomes isolated correctable holes after deinterleaving.
differentiator: Spatial reordering converts correlated damage into distributed sparse damage.

concept: A continuous cyclic signal has no marked beginning and receivers may start midstream. The player inserts a short self-unique geometric delimiter that permits reliable frame alignment.
differentiator: The problem is recovering boundaries in a valid stream, not decoding symbol meanings.

concept: A receiver occasionally misses one visible pulse according to a deterministic obstruction cycle. The player designs a request-acknowledge-retry handshake that completes exactly once without duplicate activation.
differentiator: Reliability requires feedback and duplicate suppression rather than raw redundancy.

concept: Five sensors vote on a gate, but up to two are stuck in visibly inferable patterns. The player wires a majority network whose output remains correct under every allowed fault placement.
differentiator: The construction must satisfy a fault model across cases, not the current sample only.

concept: Two senders alternate pulses on one lane with an unknown starting sender but stable alternation. Distinct pilot shapes reveal phase, allowing the player to separate and execute both commands.
differentiator: The ambiguity is multiplexed stream ownership, not compositional signal semantics.

concept: A receiver has no shared clock and advances only when signal color changes. The player re-encodes a spatial route so long repeated runs still produce enough transitions for exact recovery.
differentiator: Timing is recovered from data transitions; unchanged symbols can vanish entirely.

concept: A production line must keep moving while one module is replaced. The player routes output through a temporary bypass, synchronizes module state, then switches back without duplicating or losing items.
differentiator: Module replacement occurs during live operation and requires state handoff.

concept: Several plug-in modules share one communication stripe and collide if active together. The player assigns spatial time slots so required module pairs exchange data without bus contention.
differentiator: Connectivity is fixed and abundant; arbitration of a shared interface is the constraint.

concept: Modules expose geometric ports with direction, shape, and pulse conventions. The player chains minimal adapters so an unfamiliar sensor can drive an unfamiliar actuator.
differentiator: Compatibility spans several interface dimensions, not merely matching colors.

concept: Reversible modules function differently when flipped, and neighboring ports must alternate polarity. The player arranges a loop that performs a target transformation while every interface remains valid.
differentiator: Orientation changes both connectivity compatibility and module function.

concept: Identical grid cells can be set to route, store, transform, or block. The player configures one field to process several input patterns presented sequentially without edits.
differentiator: A homogeneous substrate must implement a reusable machine, not one fixed route.

concept: Several modules need the same unique toolhead at different phases. Moving it changes adjacency and takes turns, so the player designs a module layout and schedule around one mobile capability.
differentiator: Physical architecture and resource scheduling must be co-designed.

concept: Modules advertise effects only through demonstrations. The player discovers which outputs enable which inputs and assembles the smallest connected capability graph that realizes a requested behavior.
differentiator: The objective is minimal functional composition across opaque interfaces.

concept: The player assembles a machine from duplicated modules, then the environment disables any one module chosen after construction. The machine must still complete its task under every single failure.
differentiator: Robustness is universally tested after assembly, preventing decorative redundancy.
